sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Retirement note: Provençal spoken by Jews 'found to be indistinguishable from non-Jewish varieties of Provençal' (Pansier 1925; Banitt 1963; Guttel & Aslanov 2006). Only descriptive ref: Aslanov 2021.

sources.citation: Nahon, Peter. 2021. Modern Judeo-Provençal as Known from Its Sole Textual Testimony: Harcanot et Barcanot (Critical Edition and Linguistic Analysis). Journal of Jewish Languages 9(2): 165–237 (HAL preprint paginated 1–73). DOI 10.1163/22134638-bja10014
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: §4.2 '(Grapho)Phonetic Features' (preprint pp. 56–62) covers only three segmental traits (/ʤ/–/ʧ/ merger, -ié > -i, -íyo > -éyo); no stress rule. Stress appears only incidentally: 'final posttonic -o, following a common pattern in Provençal' (p. 49, s.v. capito); 'Hana.. As its etymon, here it is probably oxytonic (hence the retention of final -a)' (p. 54); 'nowhere is found a paroxytonic form without [-z-]' for caméyo (p. 61). 'Accent' in §4.5 (pp. 67–68) means the sociolinguistically perceived Jewish pronunciation, not word stress.

sources.citation: Guttel, Henri & Cyril Aslanov. 2007. Judeo-Provençal. Encyclopaedia Judaica, 2nd ed., vol. 11: 560 (via encyclopedia.com)
sources.note: Table of sound correspondences (l > i, ero > èyo, s > f, j/g > ch, yod > ch, metathesis); nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Szajkowski, Zosa. 1948. Dos loshn fun di Yidn in di arbe kehiles fun Komta-Venesen [The Language of the Jews in the Four Communities of Comtat Venaissin]. New York: YIVO. vii+78 pp. (Yiddish; English preface and summary pp. IV–XI)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: English summary (p. XI) only: 'we can merely give the characteristic features of the phonetics of this speech. Some of the laws (x>i) are conjecturally nothing but graphic phenomena.. Other phenomena (a>e) are not peculiar to the speech of Comtadine Jews'; segmental only (s>f), nothing on stress. Yiddish body (§XII 'Characterization of the tongue as a whole', pp. 57–76) not read: archive scanned is garbage and I did not scanned the Hebrew-script pages.

sources.citation: Pansier, P. 1925. Une comédie en argot hébraïco-provençal de la fin du XVIIIe siècle. Revue des études juives 81: 113–145
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Intro (pp. 114–115) lists four 'caractéristiques de cet argot': G doux/J > Ch; -èyo for -èro/-ilho/-iso; H for hard G; é for a in infinitives. Nothing on accent/stress.

sources.citation: Jochnowitz, George. n.d. The Importance of Judeo-Provençal for the Study of Jewish Languages (author's website essay); Jochnowitz Jewish-Languages Bibliography (same site)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Segmental chain shift (th/s/ṣ/ś > θ > f; z > ð > v; shin > s; yod > sh) and intervocalic d > z; nothing on stress. Bibliography confirms Jochnowitz 1978 (Archives juives 14: 63–67), 1985 (Brill 241–245), 2005 (Midstream).

sources.citation: Nahon, Peter. n.d. Judeo-Provençal. Jewish Language Website (HUC-JIR Jewish Language Project), with attached bibliography PDF
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Phonetic features listed are segmental only (devoicing of [dʒ]; Hebrew-pronunciation reflexes bh/gh > [u̯], s/ś/ṣ/th > [f], y > [ʧ], intervocalic ḥ > ∅). No mention of stress. Bibliography (46 items) lists no phonological or grammatical monograph on the lect.
